title: Functions

description: "Run your own code on Applad: pick a runtime, provide source, and invoke it through the API."

import { Rocket, Workflow, Send, Package } from 'lucide-react';

An Applad function is a piece of code you deploy to your project and invoke on
demand. You give Applad a **runtime** (a language and version), some **source**
(inline code or a git repository), and Applad builds a container image, keeps a
warm instance ready, and runs it when you call it. Each call is recorded as an
**execution** you can read back, so you have a history of what ran and what it
returned.

Functions are useful for work that does not belong in your client: reacting to
data, calling a third-party API with a secret, or running a scheduled job. You
can trigger a function manually through the API or on a [schedule](/build/functions#scheduling)
with a cron expression.

![The console Functions tab listing a project's functions](/screens/functions.png)
_Each function names a runtime and source; the console lists them with their status and executions._

<Callout title="Managing functions is a server task">
  Creating, updating and deleting functions changes your project's setup, so do
  it from a trusted context with your project **API key**
  (`x-applad-key: <apiKey>`), from the console, or from a deploy script, not
  from end-user code. Invoking a function is a normal authenticated request.
</Callout>

## Runtimes

A runtime is the base image your code runs on. List the built-in runtimes with
their ids:

```bash
curl https://api.applad.io/v1/functions/runtimes \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>"
```

The `id` is the value you pass as `runtime` when you create a function:

| id | Runtime |
|---|---|
| `node-18` | Node.js 18 |
| `node-20` | Node.js 20 |
| `node-22` | Node.js 22 |
| `bun-1` | Bun 1.x |
| `python-3.11` | Python 3.11 |
| `python-3.12` | Python 3.12 |
| `go-1.22` | Go 1.22 |
| `dart-3` | Dart 3.x |
| `rust-1` | Rust 1.x |
| `ruby-3` | Ruby 3.x |
| `php-8` | PHP 8.x |
| `custom` | Custom Dockerfile |

For the built-in language runtimes you provide a single source file that exports
a handler. Applad wraps it in a tiny HTTP server for you, so your code does not
need to open a port itself. Your handler receives the invocation payload as its
argument and returns a value that becomes the execution output.

<Tabs items={['Node.js', 'Python']}>
<Tab value="Node.js">

```js
// Node.js: export a function that takes the payload and returns a result
module.exports = async (payload) => {
  return { hello: payload.name || 'world' };
};
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="Python">

```python
# Python: define handler(payload) (main or default also work)
def handler(payload):
    return {"hello": payload.get("name", "world")}
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

<Callout title="Export name">
  The wrapper looks for an exported `handler`, then `main`, then `default` (Go
  and Dart use `handler`/`main`). If your source already starts its own HTTP
  server (for example an Express app that calls `listen`, or a Flask app),
  Applad detects that and runs it directly instead of wrapping it.
</Callout>

### How your source is packaged

Your inline `source` is written into the build context under a fixed filename
for its runtime, and the generated Dockerfile copies it in. This is why a single
inline file is enough: Applad knows where to put it.

| Runtime family | Source filename |
|---|---|
| `node-*` | `index.js` |
| `bun-1` | `index.ts` |
| `python-*` | `main.py` |
| `go-1.22` | `main.go` |
| `dart-3` | `main.dart` |
| others | `handler` |

The wrapper serves on port `3000` and speaks a small contract: a `POST /` hands
your handler the request body parsed as JSON and returns whatever it produces,
JSON-serialized, as the response; a `GET /` returns `ok` and is used only as a
readiness probe. Applad decides whether to wrap your code or run it as-is by
looking for server calls in the source: `listen(` or `createServer` for Node,
`serve`/`listen` for Bun, `Flask`, `uvicorn`, or `HTTPServer` for Python, and
`ListenAndServe` or `http.Handle` for Go. When one is present, your file is run
directly and is expected to listen on `3000` itself.

<Callout title="Git and multi-file sources">
  With `sourceType: "git"` the whole repository is the build context, so you are
  not limited to one file. If the repo has a `package.json` or
  `requirements.txt`, the build installs dependencies. A repo that ships its own
  server (any of the triggers above) is run directly, otherwise the same wrapper
  is applied to your entrypoint.
</Callout>

## Function lifecycle

A function moves through a short lifecycle: you create it, Applad builds and
pre-warms it, and then you invoke it and read the result back.

<Steps>

<Step>

### Creating a function

The minimum is a `name`, a `runtime`, and some source. With the client SDK you
pass inline `source`; over the REST API the inline-code field is `source` and
the source kind is `sourceType`.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart', 'cURL']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">

```ts
const fn = await client.functions.create('greet', 'node-20', {
  source: "module.exports = async (p) => ({ hello: p.name || 'world' });",
  timeout: 15,
});
const functionId = fn.$id;
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">

```dart
final fn = await client.functions.create(
  name: 'greet',
  runtime: 'node-20',
  source: "module.exports = async (p) => ({ hello: p.name || 'world' });",
  timeout: 15,
);
final functionId = fn['\$id'];
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="cURL">

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/functions \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "greet",
    "runtime": "node-20",
    "sourceType": "inline",
    "source": "module.exports = async (p) => ({ hello: p.name || \"world\" });",
    "entrypoint": "index.handler",
    "timeout": 15,
    "envVars": {}
  }'
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

The response is the function object:

```json
{
  "$id": "a1b2c3...",
  "projectId": "<projectId>",
  "name": "greet",
  "runtime": "node-20",
  "entrypoint": "index.handler",
  "timeout": 15,
  "envVars": {},
  "sourceType": "inline",
  "source": "module.exports = ...",
  "repository": "",
  "branch": "",
  "cron": "",
  "status": "building",
  "$createdAt": "2026-07-23T10:00:00Z",
  "$updatedAt": "2026-07-23T10:00:00Z"
}
```

Fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | Required. A label for the function. |
| `runtime` | Required. A runtime `id` from the list above. |
| `sourceType` | `inline` (default) or `git`. |
| `source` | Inline code, when `sourceType` is `inline`. |
| `repository` / `branch` | Git URL and branch, when `sourceType` is `git`. |
| `entrypoint` | Handler reference. Defaults to `main` on the API (`index.handler` in the SDKs). |
| `timeout` | Seconds a single execution may run. Defaults to `15`. |
| `envVars` | Map of environment variables (see [Configuration](#configuration)). |
| `cron` | Cron expression for scheduled runs, or empty for manual only. |

</Step>

<Step>

### Building

Creating or updating a function sets its `status` to `building` and pushes a
`function_build` job onto the `builds` worker queue (the same worker that holds
the Docker socket). The worker builds an image tagged `applad-fn-{functionId}`,
then pre-warms it by starting one container and sending a single warm-up
invocation before marking the function ready. That warm instance stays in a pool
so the first real call does not pay the cold-start cost. Poll the function until
its `status` is `active`:

<Tabs items={['Dart', 'cURL']}>
<Tab value="Dart">

```dart
final fn = await client.functions.get(functionId);
print(fn['status']); // building -> active
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="cURL">

```bash
curl https://api.applad.io/v1/functions/<functionId> \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>"
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

A build only runs when there is source to build (inline `source` set, or a git
`repository` set). A function created with neither stays in `building` with no
job queued.

The `status` field tracks where a function is in this cycle:

| `status` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `building` | Freshly created or updated. Image build (and pre-warm) in progress. |
| `active` | Built and pre-warmed. Ready to invoke. |
| `failed` | The build or git clone failed. Fix the source and update to rebuild. |
| `inactive` | Not currently in use. |

<Callout title="Rebuilding replaces warm instances">
  Every update re-runs the build and destroys the previous warm containers,
  because the image has changed. There is no separate deployment object or
  version history: a function has one current image, and updating it in place is
  how you ship a new version.
</Callout>

</Step>

<Step>

### Executing a function

Invoke a function by creating an execution. The call returns immediately with a
`pending` execution; the run happens on a worker.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart', 'cURL']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">

```ts
const exec = await client.functions.execute(functionId);
const executionId = exec.$id;
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">

```dart
final exec = await client.functions.execute(functionId);
final executionId = exec['\$id'];
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="cURL">

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/functions/<functionId>/executions \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{}'
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

The response:

```json
{
  "$id": "e1f2...",
  "functionId": "a1b2c3...",
  "projectId": "<projectId>",
  "status": "pending",
  "output": "",
  "errors": "",
  "duration": 0,
  "$createdAt": "2026-07-23T10:05:00Z"
}
```

Because execution is asynchronous, read the result back by fetching the
execution until its `status` is `completed` or `failed`:

<Tabs items={['Dart', 'cURL']}>
<Tab value="Dart">

```dart
final result = await client.functions.getExecution(functionId, executionId);
if (result['status'] == 'completed') {
  print(result['output']); // the response your handler returned, as a string
} else if (result['status'] == 'failed') {
  print(result['errors']);
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="cURL">

```bash
curl https://api.applad.io/v1/functions/<functionId>/executions/<executionId> \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>"
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

An execution moves through `pending` -> `processing` -> `completed` (or
`failed`). The fields on an execution object:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `$id` | Execution id. |
| `functionId` | The function that ran. |
| `status` | `pending`, `processing`, `completed`, or `failed`. |
| `output` | What your handler returned, JSON-serialized as a string. Capped at 1 MB. |
| `errors` | The error message when the run failed; empty otherwise. |
| `duration` | Wall-clock run time in seconds (a float). |
| `$createdAt` | When the execution was created. |

**What happens on the worker.** When the job is picked up the execution goes to
`processing`. Applad takes a warm container from the function's pool (or starts
one if none is free) and sends your payload as a `POST /`. A response under 400
is recorded as `completed` with the body as `output`; a `4xx`/`5xx` response, a
timeout, or a connection error is recorded as `failed`. On timeout or connection
error the container is destroyed rather than returned to the pool, since it may
be in a bad state. Idle warm containers are reaped after 5 minutes.

<Callout title="Function executions are rate limited" type="warn">
  `POST /functions/{functionId}/executions` is a project-work operation, capped
  at 300 requests per minute per project (`middleware.ProjectWorkRules`).
  Exceeding it returns `429` with "Too many function executions in the last
  minute."
</Callout>

<Callout title="Invocation payload">
  Execution runs today with an empty JSON payload (`{}`). The SDK `execute`
  methods accept a `data` argument, but that request data is not yet forwarded
  into the function, so do not rely on reading it inside your handler. Your
  handler still receives an argument, it is an empty object.
</Callout>

</Step>

</Steps>

## Providing source

### Inline

Pass your code as `source` with `sourceType: "inline"` (the default). This is
the fastest way to ship a small function and is what the SDK `source` argument
sets.

### From a git repository

Set `sourceType` to `git` and give a `repository` URL and `branch`. On build,
Applad shallow-clones the repository and builds an image from it. This suits a
function with dependencies or multiple files.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/functions \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "reporter",
    "runtime": "python-3.12",
    "sourceType": "git",
    "repository": "https://github.com/acme/reporter",
    "branch": "main",
    "timeout": 30
  }'
```

<Callout title="Private repositories">
  A public repository URL clones without any credentials. Private repositories
  need a git connection configured for your project. See [Sites](/deploy/sites) for
  how Applad connects to GitHub.
</Callout>

The client SDK `create` helper only sets inline `source`. To create a git-backed
function from an SDK, use the REST call above, or `update` with a raw body (see
[Updating and deleting](#updating-and-deleting)).

<Callout title="Custom Dockerfile">
  The runtime list includes `custom`, for supplying your own Dockerfile. The
  `create` request body does not carry a Dockerfile field today, so this path is
  not reachable through the public API yet. Use one of the language runtimes.
</Callout>

## Execution history

List every execution for a function, newest first:

<Tabs items={['Dart', 'cURL']}>
<Tab value="Dart">

```dart
final history = await client.functions.listExecutions(functionId);
for (final e in history['executions']) {
  print('${e['\$id']}: ${e['status']} (${e['duration']}s)');
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="cURL">

```bash
curl https://api.applad.io/v1/functions/<functionId>/executions \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>"
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

```json
{
  "total": 2,
  "executions": [
    { "$id": "e2...", "status": "completed", "output": "{\"hello\":\"world\"}", "duration": 0.42, "$createdAt": "..." },
    { "$id": "e1...", "status": "failed", "errors": "function returned status 500", "duration": 0.10, "$createdAt": "..." }
  ]
}
```

## Configuration

### Environment variables

Set environment variables with the `envVars` map when you create or update a
function. They are stored on the function and returned in the function object.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/functions \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "notify",
    "runtime": "node-20",
    "source": "module.exports = () => ({ ok: true });",
    "envVars": { "SLACK_WEBHOOK": "https://hooks.example.com/..." }
  }'
```

Every execution container is given `APPLAD_FUNCTION_ID` and `APPLAD_PROJECT_ID`
automatically.

<Callout title="Field name and current wiring">
  The REST field is `envVars`. The client SDK `create` helpers accept a `vars`
  argument; to be certain your variables are stored, set `envVars` explicitly
  through the REST call or an `update` with a raw body. Note that user-defined
  variables are stored on the function but are not currently injected into the
  execution container, only `APPLAD_FUNCTION_ID` and `APPLAD_PROJECT_ID` are
  guaranteed inside a run today.
</Callout>

### Timeout

`timeout` caps how long a single execution may run, in seconds (default `15`).
An execution that exceeds it is stopped and recorded as failed.

### Scheduling

Give a function a `cron` expression to run it on a schedule with no manual
trigger. Applad validates the expression when you save, so an unusable schedule
is rejected rather than silently never running. Standard 5-field expressions are
supported, along with ranges, lists, names, and a `CRON_TZ=` prefix.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/functions \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "nightly",
    "runtime": "python-3.12",
    "source": "def handler(p):\n    return {\"ran\": True}",
    "cron": "0 3 * * *"
  }'
```

An empty `cron` means the function only runs when you invoke it.

## Updating and deleting

`update` takes a raw body and re-runs the build. Send the fields you want to
change; omitted fields keep their current values (send `cron: ""` to clear a
schedule).

<Tabs items={['Dart', 'cURL']}>
<Tab value="Dart">

```dart
await client.functions.update(functionId, {
  'source': "module.exports = async (p) => ({ hi: p.name });",
  'timeout': 30,
});
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="cURL">

```bash
curl -X PUT https://api.applad.io/v1/functions/<functionId> \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "timeout": 30 }'
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

Delete a function and all of its executions:

<Tabs items={['Dart', 'cURL']}>
<Tab value="Dart">

```dart
await client.functions.delete(functionId);
```

</Tab>
<Tab value="cURL">

```bash
curl -X DELETE https://api.applad.io/v1/functions/<functionId> \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>"
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## API reference

| Method | Route | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/v1/functions/runtimes` | List built-in runtimes |
| `POST` | `/v1/functions` | Create a function |
| `GET` | `/v1/functions` | List functions |
| `GET` | `/v1/functions/{functionId}` | Get a function |
| `PUT` | `/v1/functions/{functionId}` | Update a function (re-builds) |
| `DELETE` | `/v1/functions/{functionId}` | Delete a function and its executions |
| `POST` | `/v1/functions/{functionId}/executions` | Invoke a function |
| `GET` | `/v1/functions/{functionId}/executions` | List executions |
| `GET` | `/v1/functions/{functionId}/executions/{executionId}` | Get one execution |
